s09.slug: FRIDAY · 1:15 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE BACK STEPS
body: The back steps of Hollis face the loading dock and the afternoon sun, and a dumpster that somebody in Art has painted with a dolphin, so they are warm by one o’clock and hardly anyone uses them. Jack takes the second one down with a Commons banana and his bag between his feet, forty minutes before his two o’clock.
The RAZR goes against his thigh before he has the banana open. GINA, across the little outside screen.
“Okay,” Gina says. “I have the late bus in eight minutes and I’m doing it in order.”
Behind her a row of diesels idles in the Ursuline lot with the heaters on, and a salt truck scrapes by, and a trunk slams.
“Hi, Gina.”
“Hi. Number one. Nonna. She said it nine times at breakfast. I counted under the table on my fingers. Rosie says ten, but Rosie counts the one she said to the toast.”
“It’s Mary Catherine,” Jack says.

“Not on Glenwood it isn’t. She made it Italian without being asked. She held the phone out at arm’s length like she was at the eye doctor and read it off the screen and kept going. Good crying. There’s two kinds, I’m an expert. Then she wouldn’t touch her eggs till somebody drove her to church, so we all went, before the 8:00 school Mass, and she went up the side aisle to Our Lady and put her money in and lit a tall one. Ma said *Mamma, we’ll be late*, and Nonna said *La Madonna non è mai in ritardo*, which means —”
“The Madonna’s never late.”

“I got a tardy slip for it. It says *family devotion*. And she looked up which Catherine in her missal, and it’s Alexandria. The wheel one. She out-argued fifty professors and they tried to kill her on a wheel. Nonna says Rome took her off the calendar in nineteen sixty-nine and put her back in two thousand two and never said sorry.”
“Fifty,” Jack says, to the dolphin. “Did she win all fifty?”
“Nonna said *brava*. Out loud. To a saint.”

He thinks of Skye at a red light on Thursday with Nonna’s prayer going under her breath, and of Nonna in the side aisle at St. Brigid’s with her money in her fist: two women who have never met, working the same Madonna from either end of the country. The banana is half peeled, and he has forgotten it.

“Number two. Ma. She went down to the Dell in her coat before work and looked at the picture for a full minute. I was on the stairs. It wasn’t the Tuesday face, I know the Tuesday face. She said something about her size. I’m not repeating it, she’ll say it to you herself, it’s hers.”

body.text: “And Ryan Pallante texted me. Ryan has not texted me since the fifth grade. *My mother printed your brother’s yes and put it on the refrigerator under St. Joseph.* With the period in it, Jack. He’s mortified.”

body: “And everybody at school keeps asking is she Catholic, and does she pray, and is she nice in real life, and not one of them asked about —”
“Gina.”
He pulls the banana the rest of the way open.
“— the *weather*,” Gina says. “Out there. Jeez. I was going to say the weather.”
“Number three. Did you mail it?”
“This morning. The slot in the mailroom.”
“Then it’s late. It goes in with mine Monday, and then it sits in their mailroom while a CO reads your handwriting, so it’s *very* late. That’s fine. Late’s fine. Mine has a candle on it.”

“Number four. Sunday’s Ma’s Sunday and I’m coming. Ma said yes if my chemistry’s done by Saturday night, so it will be. I’m telling him the name. In person, across the table. He’s going to *lose it*.”
“Wait till he’s eaten something.”
“Obviously after. I’m not an animal.”
Behind her the air brakes let go, and the doors fold open on their long hydraulic sigh, and a driver somewhere calls *Let’s go, ladies*.
“Bus. That’s mine — I love you, don’t tell anybody I said it on a bus.”
The doors thump shut on her end, and the RAZR goes back to being a phone.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs. Put season two in the DVD player the day after Christmas, for research, and the whole family watched. Wrote Danny about the boat. It’s a yacht. Filmed everybody’s resolutions on Theo’s Flip. Found the baptism album before I did. “Who’s the guy?” At the door, in my ear: “Don’t let Ma find out from Facebook.” Tuesday: six thousand views; Ashley Vrabel showed the whole bus. Nonna lit a candle and won’t say for who. On my wall: FINALLY — the sister who knew first. Monday she found me on a celebrity blog before I did, and knew Danny’s jacket. A man from Mahoning County called Danny a name in the comments; she reported him, answered him, and called him one back — a Catholic one. She’s making Danny a card for Candlemas. Tuesday Ashley Vrabel showed her the picture in chem. Capitals. Wednesday, at three in the morning her time: Nonna wants a baptism name, for the rosary. Friday she was lowercase again: *mary catherine?????* Nonna said it nine times at breakfast and lit a candle for her at St. Brigid’s. My Candlemas card for Danny goes in her envelope Monday. Sunday’s Ma’s Sunday. She’s telling him in person.

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees. The day after Christmas she prayed for Cassidy out loud, at the TV. *Povera.* On the Innocents she asked me to sit for the rosary, and said the intentions — for Danny, for Pop, who went in, for the nun, and for Cassidy. I told her the name’s Skye. She said Cassidy. New Year’s: lentils, a spoon each, *per i soldi*. The Befana left me coal in one of Danny’s old socks. Sugar. At the door she found me a twenty and prayed for both of us. *Tutt’e due.* Thursday night I sent Gina the name: Mary Catherine. At breakfast Nonna said *Maria Caterina* nine times, and cried the good kind, and lit a candle for her at St. Brigid’s.

s16.slug: SUNDAY · 4:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — GLENWOOD
body: A wrist corsage lies on the third step down, white, browned at the edges of the petals, left over from somebody’s Saturday. The four o’clock sun comes through the wired glass at the turn of the stairs and lays a grid across it. Jack steps over it and sits on the top landing with the RAZR open on his knee, because on Ma’s Sundays the call comes after the dishes, and the east stairwell is where Delgado keeps its bars. Down the shaft somebody drags a garment bag along a floor, a door goes, a girl laughs in a hallway at something that happened last night: the building on the afternoon after a formal.
It rings, and the little outside screen says GLENWOOD.
“Did you eat?” Ma says. “Don’t lie to me, I can hear it in your voice.”
Behind her the faucet runs, and a pan goes into the rack. “Father Dom did Nazareth at the 8:00,” she says. “A prophet’s never welcome at home. Four minutes. He was good.”
“Father Osei had that one this morning.”
“It’s the Gospel, Jackie. They don’t change it for California.” The faucet goes off. “Your father said *that’s for sure*. In the pew. Out loud.”
“Pop did?”
“Rita Pallante turned around. He looked at her till she turned back.”
Jack leans his head back against the cinderblock. In the wired glass the sun has slid down a row of the wire.
“He came in with me after, to Danny. He told him the Browns are keeping Mangini. Again. Danny put his head down on the table and said bad news is what the mail is for.”
“Ma —”

“It’s Catholic Schools Week, so there were donuts in the hall, and Rita cornered me at the donuts. Was she Catholic. I said she’s baptized. Rita said that isn’t the same thing. I said, *Rita, it’s a start.*” A cupboard, a drawer. “Your father looked at the picture over my shoulder and said *that’s a lot of limes*. Then he went to the garage.”
“It was a taquería, Ma.”
“I looked a long time. She’s tiny.”
“Ma.”
“I’m not saying anything. I’m saying somebody should feed her. It says one-thirty in the morning.”
“It had a heat lamp.”
“I saw the lamp.” A chair takes her weight. “Rosie wants to know where the crab was.”
“Tell Rosie the crab sends his regards.”

“I’m not telling her that. She’ll want to write him. Nonna’s been saying *Maria Caterina* since the 8:00. She lit another one. That’s two. Father Dom says the candle box needs a refill, and he’s not saying whose fault.”
On Glenwood Avenue the chair scrapes back. Ma says *Gina, I’m not finished*, and Gina says *you’re finished, you’re so finished*, and the phone changes size in somebody’s hand.
“Jack. It’s me. I told him. I waited till he’d had the honey bun, like you said.”
“Good.”
“I said *Mary Catherine* and he said *a NUN?* Like that. Loud. Then I told him about the picture. The lamp, the limes, your face. I did your face.”
“I don’t have a face.”
“You have *the* face. He made me do it twice. He said *oh, he’s gone.* And then he said — hold on, I have to do his voice — *ask her what she lost the bet for.*”
“What bet?”
“That’s what Ma said! He says you tricked her somehow, it’s the only explanation, and he wants to know how.”
“Tell him I didn’t trick her.”
“He said you’d say that. He said *that’s what a guy who tricked her would say.*”
Jack laughs at the wired glass, and Gina waits for him, drumming something on the table.

“And then he laughed so hard the CO came over. The big one, Jack. Ma put her hand over her eyes. The CO stood there with his newspaper, and Danny said *sorry, sir, family news*, and the CO went back. And Ma said happy birthday early, from all of us, in case your card’s late, and he said late’s a Costigan tradition. Okay. Here. Ma’s reaching.”
“Jackie.”

He hears her take a breath, the Tuesday one, from the bottom of her, and a dish towel come down on the counter. Nothing comes after it. The line holds the dishwasher and Nonna’s beads in the next room, and it goes on holding them past where a call ought to stop.
“Did you go up today?”

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition.

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me. Holy Family Sunday she took Pop in. ‘You sit, Frank.’ Showed him the machines. Goes to the seven o’clock on the last day of every year; this year I went with her. Lena called the house on the second of January, and Ma answered, and they talked for ten minutes. ‘She wants you. I don’t know why.’ Now she knows the coffee was hers. At the door she gave me the can back, empty, for the girl who called. From a gas station in Buellton I called her before I said yes on Skye’s phone. She said I was on the phone with Lena all break. I told her Lena’s still got a boyfriend, and he wrote her a song, and it was good. She didn’t say anything. Tuesday Mrs. Pallante called during dinner, and Rosie found it on the Dell before Ma got downstairs. She asked if we got married. Ma didn’t ask me what it was. She asked when I last went to confession. I said tomorrow. Then she said she’d already heard the other thing, when I said hi, so I told her: I think Skye’s the answer. Nonna heard us through the wall. ‘Go tomorrow, Jackie.’ Sunday, after the 8:00 and Trumbull: Father Dom said a prophet’s never welcome at home, and Pop said that’s for sure in the pew. She’d seen the taco picture: *she’s tiny.* Then one question — did I go up today. I said yes. She said good.

choices.text: “I went up, Ma. With her there.”
response: “With her there,” Ma says, trying it. A cupboard shuts. “Did she stay in the pew?”
“Good.” It comes out of her on a long breath, all the way down.
Through the wall Nonna goes on with the decade, and drops the name into it again, *Maria Caterina*, at the end of every Hail Mary, like a bell.

choices.text: “Tell Nonna thank you. For the candle.”
response: “Yes, Ma,” he says. “And tell Nonna thank you. For the candle.”
Ma tells her, with her hand nowhere near the phone: “Mamma, Jackie says thank you for the candle.” From the front room Nonna answers with something short in dialect, and Ma does not translate it.
“Good,” Ma says, about all of it.
“Good.” It comes out of her a half-step higher than anything she has said yet.
The dishwasher starts to fill. “Eat something real,” Ma says over it, and then there is only the water.
